summary:
Schleswig-Holstein stands under the German national framework. Legal gender recognition runs through the Self-Determination Act (SBGG), in force since 1 November 2024, under which a prisoner's placement tracks the legal gender entry unless Länder law provides an exclusion.

No Schleswig-Holstein statute or ordinance specific to trans people is in force. The state has no prison act provision of its own governing the placement of trans prisoners, so the SBGG mechanics and the national July 2026 placement case are the operative rules for a visitor detained here.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure. In July 2026 a German court sent a person convicted of neo-Nazi incitement, whose legal gender had been changed to female under the Self-Determination Act, to a men's prison, amid public outcry over women's-prison safety. The case drove the Länder-level prison-placement law debate.

Constitutional doubt about that debate is on the record. A Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 raised constitutional objections to trans-targeted exception clauses in Länder prison law.
tangentialFactors:
Protection machinery runs partly through the Länder. Schleswig-Holstein, with Hesse, Berlin, Bremen and Saarland, tabled a joint motion in the Bundesrat for a ban on conversion therapy, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019, and reported ahead of that week by Zeit Online on 10 April 2019. Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia supported the motion and Bavaria indicated potential support with modifications; the Bundestag approved the federal ban on 7 May 2020 with backing from every party except the AfD.

Germany's wider exposure profile is documented in cases arising in other Länder: a DJ and producer filed a legal complaint under the Equal Treatment Act over an airport screening on 23 November 2024 in which officers allegedly disregarded her gender identity, characterising it as targeted transphobic harassment. A visitor transiting a German airport faces the same screening apparatus that produced the complaint.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off public argument over trans women's access to such venues, argument that Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel reported on for Berlin saunas and similar spaces.

Reporting and support machinery for hostility encountered in country exists outside Schleswig-Holstein's own borders but is usable from there: the STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation in northern Germany, provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.
localsOnly:
Residents held in Schleswig-Holstein's prison system are placed under the German national prison regime, in which statutory housing is separated on a men and women binary and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been applied only in exceptional cases. Because Schleswig-Holstein has not legislated its own rule, the SBGG default and the federal placement precedent govern, with no state-level exclusion clause to override them.

Residents seeking legal gender recognition do so under the SBGG declaration procedure at the local registrar, the same route used nationwide since 1 November 2024; the resulting entry is what drives any downstream placement question.

Residents may draw on the counselling and reporting infrastructure listed above, including the northern German counselling finder and crisis line, for hostility encountered within the state.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no Schleswig-Holstein-specific prison placement statistics, no recorded incidents of trans prisoners housed in the state, and no record of how the SBGG default has actually been applied in a Schleswig-Holstein facility; whether the July 2026 placement precedent is followed here remains unverified.

The Verfassungsblog constitutional objection concerns Länder prison law generally; the inventory does not state whether any court has ruled on it, and whether Schleswig-Holstein would face litigation over a placement exclusion it has not enacted is unresolved.

Whether the federal conversion therapy ban covers gender identity, or only sexual orientation, is not stated in the sources; the claim is confined here to what is sourced: the joint Bundesrat motion of April 2019 and the Bundestag vote of 7 May 2020.
